blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.

blocks.en: 1  Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Video is the most abundant record of how agents act in the physical world,
spanning robots of many embodiments, human manipulation, and simulation. Much of
it cannot serve directly as action supervision, since egocentric human video
provides no robot action labels and robot datasets record actions in
embodiment-specific spaces. Latent action models
(LAMs) [ 71 , 9 , 94 ] address this gap. An
inverse-dynamics model (IDM) infers a latent action from an observed change, and
a forward-dynamics model (FDM) reproduces the change from it. The resulting shared
action space is used to pretrain vision-language-action (VLA)
policies [ 94 , 11 , 20 , 62 , 45 ] and to control world models [ 29 , 30 , 74 ] .

blocks.en:
We start from a simple observation. A video world model is natively an FDM
( Fig. 1 b). Pretrained on large-scale robot and human video, it
carries a strong forward-dynamics prior on how scenes evolve, renders the future
faithfully, and implicitly captures inverse dynamics, which world action models (WAMs) exploit
to decode actions [ 46 , 108 , 44 , 95 ] . A
pretrained world model can thus be viewed as a unified LAM whose learning signal
need not be spent on rendering. Its dynamics, however, are entangled with
appearance across dense hidden states, with no compact representation from which
actions can be read. The challenge is to expose these dynamics natively through
a compact action interface.

Native LAM ( Fig. 1 c) appends a short, temporally ordered sequence
of learnable dynamics registers to a pretrained video diffusion
transformer and runs it in two modes, with no separate encoder or decoder and
the registers as the only causal bridge between them. In IDM mode , the
registers read a clean clip and yield the latent action. In FDM mode , the
same network regenerates the future from the first frame and this latent alone,
with its original flow-matching objective and no text. Training on counterfactual temporal pairs , clips that share a first frame but differ
in motion, forces the latent to carry the motion. We term the resulting
representation native latent actions, as it is produced and consumed by
the world model itself rather than an auxiliary encoder–decoder pair.
Native LAM thereby condenses the thousands of high-dimensional tokens that the
world model processes for a clip (3,456 tokens of dimension 2,560, using Kairos 3.1 [ 37 ] as the
pretrained video DiT) into 32 latent
action tokens of dimension 128, without changing the network architecture or adding
a separate encoder or decoder.

We validate native latent actions in two respects. Quantitatively, they
outperform existing LAMs in both action classification and control regression
on the LARY benchmark ( Sec. 4.2.1 ). Qualitatively, a latent action extracted from
a robot video and replayed in FDM mode from a different first frame reproduces
the same motion in a new scene, on another robot, or with a human hand
( Fig. 1 d), although training uses no transfer objective.

blocks.en: 2  Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Latent action models. LAPO [ 71 ] and Genie [ 9 ] showed that an IDM/FDM pair trained to reconstruct future observations recovers
a latent action space from unlabeled video. Most later
LAMs [ 94 , 11 , 20 , 100 , 41 , 97 , 30 , 49 ] follow this recipe and train their IDM and FDM from scratch. Nikulin et al . [ 60 ] show that, with distractors, the latents tend to
collapse onto pixel change.
Many LAMs further constrain the latent during
training. LAPA [ 94 ] and Moto [ 21 ] quantize it into tokens,
RotVLA [ 45 ] models it as rotations, ALAM [ 78 ] regularizes it for composition and reversal consistency, and UniVLA [ 11 ] conditions it
on language. villa-X [ 20 ] adds proprioceptive supervision, which is closest to our
kinematic grounding.
Latent actions serve world models. AdaWorld [ 29 ] and
DreamDojo [ 30 ] use them as the control input of world models learned from
unlabeled video, and LD4WAM [ 74 ] learns latent dynamics from
human video and distills them from generated futures to condition a world
action model. In these methods the latent actions serve a world model but are
still extracted by a separate LAM. Native LAM reverses this relation: the
world model itself extracts the latent action, and its own generator is the
decoder.

blocks.en:
World models for policy learning. Pretrained video generators such as Wan [ 83 ] and robot-oriented
world models such as Kairos [ 37 ] encode strong dynamics priors, and
several lines of work bring them into policy learning. Video-as-policy methods generate a future and recover actions with an inverse-dynamics
model [ 26 , 79 ] . World action models train a video
generator and an action generator jointly, so that one model predicts both
future frames and actions [ 46 , 108 , 47 , 13 , 40 , 44 , 74 , 8 , 12 , 15 , 53 ] ;
Fast-WAM [ 95 ] shows that much of their benefit comes from video
co-training rather than test-time imagination; it keeps video generation as a
training objective and skips it at inference. Alignment methods instead
supervise the policy, or its future tokens, with representations of future
observations—generated images [ 103 ] , video-model
features [ 34 ] , or frozen-encoder embeddings [ 107 , 101 , 3 , 55 , 66 ] .
In all three, the policy is tied to dense visual targets that are dominated by
appearance, which recent studies identify as a source of brittleness under
visual shift [ 55 , 66 ] . Native LAM uses the world
model differently: it distills the model’s dynamics into a compact latent
action, and PAWlicy aligns to that latent alone, so the policy neither
renders pixels nor carries a video backbone.

blocks.en:
Visual representations for action. Self-supervised image and video encoders [ 75 , 4 ] are widely used as visual backbones for policies. LARY [ 59 ] probes such encoders and LAMs for semantic actions and low-level robot
control. Encoder features are dense, with hundreds of patch tokens per frame,
whereas a latent action is a compact bottleneck of a few tokens per segment.
We therefore compare with embodied LAMs under LARY’s protocol and show that a
compact world-model-derived latent action is more action-informative than
existing ones.

PAWlicy is a pretraining paradigm in which the trained Native LAM acts as
a frozen dynamics teacher. The teacher assigns native latent actions to every
video, irrespective of whether actions were recorded, and a VLA is trained to
predict these latents and to condition its actions on them. We instantiate the
paradigm with three experts that share attention ( Fig. 3 ): a
vision-language model (VLM) that encodes the observation and instruction, a latent action DiT that predicts native latent actions, and an action DiT that generates motor commands.

blocks.en:
Reconstructing the past to predict the future. The VLM is pretrained for vision-language understanding, and its
representations are not trained to match the latent space of Native LAM.
Predicting future latents directly from them asks the latent action DiT to map
into this space and to forecast dynamics that have not yet been observed, all
at once. We ease this by adding a past latent group to the target and a past
frame to the input. Native LAM encodes eight groups per clip; we truncate the target 𝐚 ^ t ∗ \hat{\mathbf{a}}^{*}_{t} to the first four, which keeps the prediction horizon of
PAWlicy close to that of common VLAs: one group for the
segment that has just been observed and three for the segments that follow. In addition,
the VLM receives, besides the current image, a past frame from the beginning
of the observed segment. Recovering the
past group from the two images is an inverse-dynamics problem whose answer is
contained in the input. This reconstruction objective therefore provides a dense
and well-posed signal that encourages the VLM output to align with the latent
space, and lets the future groups, which are generated jointly with it,
continue from a latent anchored in what has already been observed. Beyond using the past frame for this reconstruction, the
latent action DiT must also predict reliably when no past frame is available,
as at the start of an episode. We therefore drop the past frame at random, and
additionally at the start of an episode during fine-tuning.

are decoded back into the clip they were read from, frame by frame and for the

(third frame of Fig. 6 a). Native LAM reconstructs both large and small motions sharply, which we attribute to the
prior of its pretrained world model, and the generated motion follows the
source. For the whole clip ( Fig. 6 b), the frame-pair LAMs must roll out autoregressively,
so their errors accumulate and within a few steps the arm and the banana blur
away or stop moving. Native LAM generates the clip in one pass, which these
LAMs cannot do directly, and keeps the arm, the banana, and the motion intact
to the end.

blocks.en: 5  Conclusion and Future Work
blocks.zh: 5 结论和今后的工作

blocks.en:
We show that a pretrained video world model can serve as a native latent action
model. Through dynamics registers, Native LAM distills motion information
entangled with appearance into a compact latent that transfers across scenes and
embodiments and interpolates into coherent intermediate motions. As a frozen
teacher, it enables PAWlicy to learn from robot, human, and simulated video
without generating video during policy training or inference, improving a
generalist VLA in simulation and on a real robot.

blocks.en:
This study establishes the paradigm on Kairos 3.1. Only two of 46 training
sources provide kinematic grounding; the remainder are video-only, and the
evaluation datasets contain no overlapping trajectories, indicating that the
learned action structure is not simply inherited from dense action labels. The
transfer experiments preserve initial geometry while varying embodiment, scene,
or domain, providing a controlled qualitative test of motion retention. Future
work will test other video DiTs, isolate the contribution of kinematic
grounding, and evaluate broader geometric changes and additional robots. As
video world models improve, their internal dynamics may provide an increasingly
scalable foundation for learning actions from video.

本研究确立了凯罗斯3.1的范式. 46次培训中只有2次
来源提供动能地面;其余仅限视频;
评价数据集没有重叠的轨迹,表明
所学的动作结构并不仅仅是从密集的动作标签中继承的. 这个
转移实验保留了最初的几何特征,而不同的表现,场景,
或域,对运动保留提供受控的质量测试. 未来
工作将测试其他视频 DiTs, 孤立动能的贡献
定位,并评价更广泛的几何变化和额外的机器人. 作为
视频世界模式有所改善,其内部动态可能日益提供
从视频中学习动作的可扩展基础.
